description: The Sunni six articles of faith versus the Shi'a Five Roots, and the key divides between them.
content_html:
What Do Muslims Believe?

Islam is a complete way of life built on a set of core convictions about God, revelation, prophethood and the future. These convictions are not simply ideas to hold in the mind — they shape prayer, behaviour, community and identity. Two major traditions within Islam, Sunni Islam and Shi’a Islam, express these convictions through different but overlapping frameworks of belief.

The Six Articles of Faith in Sunni Islam

Sunni Muslims organise their essential beliefs into six articles of faith. Together they form the backbone of Sunni identity. The Qur’an states: “Whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day has gone far astray” (Surah 4:136). Each article carries its own weight:

  • Belief in Allah — the one God, without partner or equal. Islam teaches that Allah transcends all human perception: “No vision can grasp Him, but His grasp is over all vision” (Surah 6:103), emphasising that Allah is beyond the reach of human senses.
  • Belief in angels (mala’ikah) — created from light, carrying out Allah’s commands.
  • Belief in the holy books (kutub) — the scriptures revealed to the prophets, of which the Qur’an is the final, undistorted form.
  • Belief in the prophets (nabi/rasul) — messengers chosen by Allah to guide humanity.
  • Belief in the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din) — when every soul will be called to account for its deeds.
  • Belief in predestination (al-Qadr) — that Allah’s knowledge encompasses all things, past, present and future. The Hadith of Sahih Muslim (Book 33, Hadith 6400) affirms that belief in divine decree — both its good and its seemingly difficult aspects — is a pillar of faith.
Key Fact

The six articles of faith for Sunni Muslims are: Allah, angels, holy books, prophets, the Day of Judgement, and predestination. Surah 4:136 references five of the six, making it a key verse for this topic.

Usul ad-Din: The Five Roots of Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims express their foundational beliefs through the concept of Usul ad-Din, the principles of faith. These five roots are:

  • Al-Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah. Everything else flows from this.
  • Al-Adl — divine justice. Allah is perfectly fair in all His actions and judgements.
  • Al-Nubuwwah — prophethood. Allah communicates with humanity through chosen prophets.
  • Al-Imamah — the Imamate, or divinely appointed leadership. After the Prophet Muhammad, spiritual and political authority passed to the Imams from his family.
  • Al-Ma’ad — resurrection and the Day of Judgement. The Qur’an warns: “Every soul is held responsible for what it has earned” (Surah 74:38), pointing to an individual reckoning after death.
Key Fact

The Five Roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi’a Islam are: Al-Tawhid (oneness), Al-Adl (justice), Al-Nubuwwah (prophethood), Al-Imamah (leadership), Al-Ma’ad (resurrection). These are distinct from the Sunni six articles; confusing the two is a common exam error.

Justice and Imamate: The Key Differences

Two of the Five Roots have no direct equivalent in the Sunni six articles: Al-Adl and Al-Imamah. These are specifically Shi’a emphases and lie at the heart of the historical division between the two communities.

For Shi’a Muslims, justice is not just one of Allah’s attributes but a defining principle of how the universe operates. Allah is incapable of injustice, which means that suffering and hardship can be understood as purposeful tests rather than random events. This belief gives the Shi’a community a distinctive theological lens through which to interpret human history and the will of God.

The Imamate is the Shi’a belief that after the Prophet Muhammad’s death, leadership of the Muslim community passed to a succession of twelve Imams, beginning with Ali ibn Abi Talib. These Imams are considered to be free from sin and error (infallible) and are the authoritative interpreters of the Qur’an and Islamic law.

Sunni Muslims do not accept this doctrine. They hold that the community should be guided by the consensus of scholars and the Sunnah (the Prophet’s example), rather than by a hereditary line of Imams. The Qur’an instructs believers to “obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you” (Surah 4:59), but Sunni and Shi’a interpret “those in authority” differently. The Hadith al-Thaqalayn, widely cited by Shi’a Muslims, records the Prophet urging his followers to hold fast to both the Qur’an and his household — a text used to support the special authority of the Imams.

Common Ground and Divergent Emphases

Despite these differences, Sunni and Shi’a Muslims share a great deal. Both affirm Tawhid (the oneness of God), the prophethood of Muhammad, the Qur’an as the final revealed scripture, the five daily prayers, and the expectation of a Day of Judgement. The differences lie mainly in how authority, leadership and justice are understood and structured — not in the fundamental beliefs about God Himself.

Sunni six articles: Allah • Angels • Holy Books • Prophets • Day of Judgement • Predestination (al-Qadr). Framework: beliefs held individually and collectively by all Muslims.

Shi’a Five Roots (Usul ad-Din): Al-Tawhid • Al-Adl • Al-Nubuwwah • Al-Imamah • Al-Ma’ad. The emphasis on justice (Al-Adl) and the Imamate (Al-Imamah) are unique to this framework. Both traditions share the first and last of these concepts in different forms.

A common misconception is that Shi’a Muslims do not believe in predestination. In fact, they do accept divine knowledge, but the Mu’tazilite school of thought (historically influential in Shi’a theology) emphasised human free will more strongly, believing that predestination which removes human responsibility would be unjust — and therefore impossible for a just God.
exam_tip_html: Examiners frequently reward students who distinguish clearly between the Sunni six articles of faith and the Shi’a Five Roots of Usul ad-Din. A very common error is to attribute the Five Roots to Sunni Islam, or to list predestination as a Shi’a Root (it is not — Al-Qadr appears in the Sunni framework). For a 15-mark Discuss question, make sure you can argue both that the differences between Sunni and Shi’a belief are fundamental (justice, Imamate) AND that both traditions share the same core convictions about Allah, prophethood and the afterlife. SPaG marks are awarded on extended responses, so spell key terms accurately: ‘Tawhid’, ‘Usul ad-Din’, ‘Imamah’, ‘al-Qadr’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sunni Muslims follow six articles of faith: belief in Allah, angels, holy books, prophets, the Day of Judgement, and predestination (al-Qadr). Surah 4:136 is the key Qur’anic anchor.
  • Shi’a Muslims follow the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din: Al-Tawhid, Al-Adl, Al-Nubuwwah, Al-Imamah and Al-Ma’ad. The Imamate and divine justice are the distinctly Shi’a emphases.
  • Both traditions share core convictions about God, prophethood and the afterlife; the key divergence is in authority and leadership after the Prophet, with Shi’a Muslims believing in the divine appointment of twelve Imams.

practice_questions.text: State the name given to the Shi'a framework of five foundational beliefs.
Describe what Muslims mean by 'the six articles of faith'.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a response that includes: the six articles are the core beliefs that Sunni Muslims must hold (1 mark); they include belief in Allah, angels, holy books, prophets, the Day of Judgement and predestination/al-Qadr (1 mark for naming at least two correctly, or for a clear description of their function as a framework of belief). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of the following correctly named and briefly described: Al-Tawhid (the oneness of Allah); Al-Adl (divine justice); Al-Nubuwwah (prophethood); Al-Imamah (the Imamate or divinely appointed leadership); Al-Ma'ad (resurrection and the Day of Judgement). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Shi'a concept of the Imamate differs from Sunni beliefs about leadership in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Possible content: Shi'a Muslims believe that after the Prophet Muhammad, leadership passed to a line of twelve divinely appointed Imams descended from the Prophet's family, beginning with Ali; Sunni Muslims do not accept hereditary divine leadership and hold that the community is guided by the consensus of scholars and the Sunnah (1+1 mark for point and development). The twelve Imams in Shi'a belief are considered infallible interpreters of scripture and law; Sunni scholars do not claim infallibility (1+1 mark). The Hadith al-Thaqalayn is cited by Shi'a Muslims to support the special authority of the Prophet's household; Sunni Muslims interpret this hadith differently (1+1 mark). [6 marks: 3 marks per point — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'The differences between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims are more significant than what they share.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Imamate (Al-Imamah) is a uniquely Shi'a belief with no Sunni equivalent — it changes the entire structure of religious authority; Al-Adl (divine justice) as a root of faith is absent from the Sunni framework; historical divisions over leadership after the Prophet led to lasting community separation; different hadith collections and legal schools reflect genuinely divergent traditions. Arguments against: Both traditions hold Tawhid as the most fundamental belief; both accept the prophethood of Muhammad and the authority of the Qur'an; both expect a Day of Judgement and hold similar eschatological beliefs; the Five Pillars are shared in practice; the six articles and five roots overlap significantly in content (Allah, prophethood, afterlife). Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Surah 4:136, Hadith al-Thaqalayn, Surah 74:38), explicit weighing of the significance of shared vs divergent beliefs, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides developed with some reference to sources; conclusion present. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence; one-sided or limited. Emerging: Brief, one-sided, little evidence. [15 marks: 10 AO1 + 5 AO2; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: State one belief that is unique to Shi'a Islam and not found in the Sunni six articles of faith.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: Al-Adl (divine justice) / Al-Imamah (the Imamate / belief in divinely appointed Imams). [1 mark]

knowledge_checks.q: How many articles of faith do Sunni Muslims hold?
Which of the following is a root of Shi'a Usul ad-Din that has NO direct equivalent in the Sunni six articles?
options: Belief in the Day of Judgement

knowledge_checks.q: The Shi'a framework of foundational beliefs is called _____.
Surah 4:136 is the key Qur'anic verse used to support the _____ articles of faith in Sunni Islam.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: Divine justice — a uniquely Shi'a root of faith
The divinely appointed leadership of the Imams
Resurrection and the Day of Judgement

flashcard_questions.q: How many articles of faith do Sunni Muslims follow?
flashcard_questions.a: Six — Allah, angels, holy books, prophets, Day of Judgement, predestination.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Arabic name for the Shi'a framework of five foundational beliefs?
Which Qur'anic verse names five of the six Sunni articles of faith?
Name the five roots of Shi'a Usul ad-Din.
What does Al-Adl mean, and which tradition holds it as a root of faith?
flashcard_questions.a: Divine justice; it is a distinctly Shi'a root with no Sunni equivalent.
The Shi'a belief in divinely appointed, infallible Imams descended from the Prophet's family.

flashcard_questions.q: Which hadith is cited by Shi'a Muslims to support the authority of the Prophet's household?
What is al-Qadr, and in which framework does it appear?
flashcard_questions.a: Predestination — the sixth Sunni article of faith, not a Shi'a root.
Resurrection and the Day of Judgement, the fifth Shi'a root.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one belief that Sunni and Shi'a Muslims hold in common.
flashcard_questions.a: Any one: Tawhid (oneness of Allah), prophethood of Muhammad, the Qur'an as final scripture.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Usul ad-Din mean in English?
Which Shi'a root emphasises that Allah is incapable of injustice?

glossary_terms.definition: The largest branch of Islam, whose members follow the six articles of faith and the Sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad.
The second largest branch of Islam, whose members emphasise the authority of the Imams descended from the Prophet's family.
The six core beliefs that every Sunni Muslim must hold: belief in Allah, angels, holy books, the prophets, the Day of Judgement, and predestination.
An Arabic phrase meaning 'the principles of faith', used in Shi'a Islam to describe the five roots that form the basis of belief.
The Shi'a belief that divine justice is a fundamental attribute of Allah, who never acts unjustly.
The Shi'a doctrine that religious and political leadership after the Prophet belonged to a line of divinely guided Imams from his family.
The line of divinely appointed leaders in Shi'a Islam, descended from the Prophet Muhammad through his son-in-law Ali, believed to be infallible guides for the community.
